title: Chapter 196 – The Hall's Last Door
html:
[The Root Cellar and the Dock – Lin Jian]

Two girls stand in the snow, and neither of them knows which one is the copy.

Jian watches it from the orchard gate with his back against the cold wooden post, because his legs have stopped being reliable. The sun is a low white coin behind the cloud. The tree is singing very softly. Around the open cellar a ring of people has formed, a hundred or more, shivering in their cloaks and quilts and saying nothing at all. A baby cries somewhere and is hushed. The Warden's stone hand rests on the black iron ring of the cellar door, and the light-stair beneath it has begun to fade, a step at a time, like a candle burning down.

In the middle of the snow, Ethan Cole kneels with the small girl in his arms. He has not let go of her. She has one arm around his neck and the other around her one-eared rabbit, and she is looking across his shoulder at the older girl who has slid down from Duan Ke's back.

"Hello," says the small one.

"Hello," says Mei. Her voice is barely a breath. She is six percent. She is the color of mist. She walks across the snow with the care of someone carrying a full cup, and stops an arm's length away.

"You have my face."

"I know."

"You're big."

"I'm eleven."

"I'm five." The child considers this with fierce attention. "Are you my sister?"

Mei opens her mouth. Jian sees her try to say it. Sees the word no and the word yes and the word I don't know crowd into her throat, each trying to push the others out. She looks at her father. Ethan is weeping silently, with his chin on the small girl's head, and he does not seem to have heard the question.

"I'm the one who stayed," says Mei at last.

"Stayed where?"

"In the dark. With the lamps." She tries to smile. "Somebody had to keep them lit."

"Was it scary?"

"Sometimes."

"I was scared," says the small girl, with great dignity. "At first. And then the voice sang to me, and it wasn't so bad." She leans out of her father's arms, tilting dangerously, and holds out the rabbit. "You can hold him. His name is Mr. Ear."

Mei looks at the rabbit. Her eyes fill.

"Mr. Ear," she says. "I remember him."

* * *

The Interface wakes in Jian's skull as soon as the two palms touch.

He did not call it. It simply rises, as a tide rises, and his vision gives a small silver flicker as the panel opens at the edge of his sight. He lets his head tip back against the post. He is too tired to stop it.

```
ARK-7 // ANOMALY
TWO PATTERNS ........ SAME ORIGIN
SUBJECT A: MEI (KEPT, 11 YRS APPARENT, 6%)
SUBJECT B: MEI (BLOOM-HELD, 5 YRS APPARENT, 100%)
CORRELATION ........ 0.98 (CHILDHOOD)
DIVERGENCE ......... 6 YEARS (A: DEAD BODY, KEPT / B: LIVE BODY, HELD)
NOTE: SUBJECT B HAS A BODY.
```

He reads the last line twice. A body. Not a pattern, not a projection of light. Warm flesh, a pulse, a child's lungs full of cold air. He looks at her again and sees the faint rise and fall of her chest, the pink in her cheeks, the way she squints in the sun.

The Bloom did not keep a copy. It kept her.

We made a thing that ate a world, he thinks, and in the middle of the eating, it held one child's hand.

```
ARK-7 // QUERY
HOST HAS PRINT UNLOCKED.
SUBJECT A COULD BE MERGED INTO SUBJECT B.
COST ESTIMATE: 10 YEARS OF HOST LIFESPAN. CORE INTEGRITY -9%.
NOTE: MERGE IS IRREVERSIBLE.
NOTE: THE CHOICE IS NOT THE HOST'S.
```

He almost laughs. The thing in his head has learned a new kind of tact.

No, he thinks. It is not mine.

He pushes himself off the post.

* * *

It takes the rest of the afternoon, and no one hurries it.

They bring the girls to the kitchen, because the kitchen is where one takes anyone who has had a shock. Qinghe puts the small one on a stool by the hearth with a mug of warm milk and sits beside her, and the small one drinks it all and wipes her mouth on her sleeve. Mei sits at the end of the bench with her hands folded in her lap and the leaf from the Mother Tree in her palm. Ethan has been put in the big chair by the fire, with a blanket over his knees. He is down to a fifth of what he was. He sits with his silver hands open on the blanket, looking from one daughter to the other, and does not speak.

It is Mo Yan who finally breaks the silence.

She slips off the bench and walks to the small Mei and puts out her hand. The child looks at it, then takes it. For a moment they stand there, a mute girl of eight and a bright-eyed girl of five, palm to palm. The air between them shimmers.

"She's glad," says Yue softly, from the door. She has her bandaged hand pressed to her chest. "She says the little one is glad to be asked."

"Asked what?" says the small girl.

"If you want to stay," says Yue. "Here. In the valley. Or go somewhere else."

The five-year-old frowns. She looks at her father, then at the big girl, then at Qinghe, who is stirring the pot and trying not to be seen to listen.

"Can Papa come?"

Ethan makes a small broken sound.

"I think," says Qinghe gently, "that you should ask him."

The child climbs down from her stool. She pads across the flagstones in her too-long gown, and climbs into her father's lap as though she had done it all her life, and puts her forehead against his.

"Are you coming?" she says.

"If you want."

"Will it hurt?"

"No."

"You said that last time."

"Did I?" He laughs, wet and helpless. "I'm sorry, sweetheart. I was wrong a great many times. I'd like very much to stop."

She nods, grave as a judge. Then she turns her head and looks at Mei, across the fire-bright room.

"You too," she says. "You have to come too."

Mei does not answer. She is looking at the child's hand where it rests on Ethan's silver sleeve, small and brown and solid, and Jian knows exactly what she is thinking, because he is thinking it too.

* * *

She comes to him at dusk, in the pantry, alone.

He has taken refuge there with a cup of Bell's black wax tea, because it is the one room in the house with a door that locks. He is sitting on the same barrel he has sat on a dozen times this month, with his staff across his knees and his back against the sacks. The lamp on its hook is guttering. He does not trim it.

"I thought you'd be here," says Mei.

"I am predictable."

"You are tired." She sits on the flour sack, leaving a gap between them. She is a very faint thing now, a pale hum in the dark. "I need to ask you something. And I need you not to lie."

"I will do my best."

"That's the lying kind of answer."

"Yes." He tips his head back against the sacks. "Ask."

"The Interface told you something." Her voice is steady. "It told you a way to fix this. I felt it. When I touched her, a door opened in the air, and you were reading it. What did it say?"

He is silent for a long moment. He thinks of lying. He thinks of Yue in the alley, of the second lie he told in a single day.

"That I could put you into her," he says.

Mei goes quite still.

"Into the small one. Her body is real. Her pattern is yours, or as near as makes no difference. If I printed the merge, you would go into her, and she would go into you, and there would be one girl." He turns the cup in his hands. "It would cost ten years of my life and a piece of the core. It is irreversible."

"And she'd be me."

"She would be you, and she would be five, and she would not remember most of what you have done. She would remember your father. She would remember the leaf." He swallows. "She would be warm."

"And I would be..."

"Not here. In the way you are here."

Mei looks at her own hands. They are almost transparent. She turns them over, one and then the other, and the lamp shows through the bones.

"Would it hurt her?"

"The Interface says no."

"Would it hurt me?"

"I do not know."

"Do you think I should?"

"No." The word comes out quicker than he intended. "Mei, I think you should not, if you are asking me. I think you should say no, and keep what you are. Because I have watched you be a person for a year, and I would not give that up for a better body."

"Even though I'm dying."

"You are not dying." He leans forward. "You are spent. There is a difference. Spent things can be filled. Your father, the tree, the Hall, they have a great deal of time. They can fill you slowly, in a way that is yours. I think that is the choice that is not a trap."

"And her?"

"She is a child, and she is warm. She will grow. She will be with your father, who has been a ghost for six hundred years and is going to need a great many hours of being loved." His voice cracks. "She does not need to be you. She needs to be herself."

Mei is quiet.

"That's three reasons for me not to do it," she says at last. "Are there any for?"

"One," says Jian. "That it would be easier."

She laughs, a thin, helpless laugh, and puts her hand to her mouth.

"I think I'll take the hard one," she says. "I'm used to it."

* * *

Han's grain arrives in the gray hour before dawn.

Jian hears it before he sees it, a long creak and rumble of wheels down the valley road, and he goes out in his cloak with his staff to find the whole clan already gathered at the gate. Forty wagons. Each one is drawn by a pair of shaggy brown mules, and each is piled high with sacks under oiled canvas. At the head of the line, on the seat of the first, sits a square, stern woman in a gray quilted gown with the Keeper's seal on her breast.

"Head Han," says Zhao, hurrying out with his ledger. His breath smokes. "You are early."

"I was told it was an emergency." Han climbs down with the economy of long habit. She nods to Jian, a curt dip of the chin, and looks past him at the open cellar on the hill, at the silver tree, at the queer pale crowd of children by the gate. "Twelve thousand measures. The first wave. The rest follows by the new moon."

"Head," says Zhao, in a strangled voice. "I do not think you understand. We have nine million—"

"Ninety." She lifts one eyebrow. "I understand you have ninety days of grain and a Hall full of sleepers who say they wish to wake. I was told it by Elder Gu. He had it from a crow." The corner of her mouth moves. "Do not look so shocked, Steward. The Wall hears a good deal. And I have a standing offer, I believe, that has not yet been withdrawn."

Jian stands there with the cold in his hands. He thinks of Han on her own battlement, a hundred and fifty days ago, saying that a wall is a promise you keep every day or not at all.

"The Seat of the Keeper of Walls," he says.

"I never meant it as a bribe." Her gaze is level. "I meant it as a door."

Behind him, he hears the clan begin to cheer. It starts as a mutter and rolls through the crowd like a wave, and in a moment Kuang is up on the wagon bed waving his hat and Elder Mu's old guard are hammering their spears on the gate, and the mules, startled, begin to bray. Yue is laughing. Wenyuan has taken off his hat. Qinghe, at the kitchen door, has put down her ladle and begun, quite openly, to weep.

Han looks at it all. For the space of a breath, her stern face softens.

"Do not make me regret it," she says.

"I will try."

"Try harder." She turns back to the wagons. "Unload. We have a great deal of barley to count."

* * *

They hold the Council the next morning, nine chairs in the unlit chamber, and the small girl sits in the tenth.

It is not a real chair. Cheng Hui carried a stool in from the kitchen and covered it with a quilt, and Duan Ke lashed a back to it out of firewood, and the result is lopsided and charming. She sits on it with her feet tucked under her and Mr. Ear in her lap, wide-eyed, watching everyone.

"I don't know what to say," says Cheng Hui, and the others laugh. "I'm serious. We have a seat for the Warden's daughter. We have a seat for the Founders' Bell. There's no ruling for a tenth."

"I'm not a Nine," says the small girl, with dignity. "I'm Mei."

"There are two of you."

"Then I'll be Little Mei."

"She can be Little Mei," says Mei from her chair. "It's what I called her in my head when I was small. It's fine."

The room lets out a breath. Tian Mo stands at the door with his stone arm folded and a look on his face as if he has been handed a very good loaf of bread. At the table's head, Ethan Cole sits on a plain stool at the table's head. They have set him there. He asked to be. His light is faint, a slender silver outline, and when he lifts his hand to speak, the Council's lamps lean toward him.

"I have a request," he says.

"Go ahead."

"I would like to be allowed to die."

The room goes silent.

"Not at once," says Ethan, quickly. "I have no wish to leave the girls before they are ready. But I have been alive for six hundred years, and for most of them I did not deserve to be. I have a wife in a tree who has asked me to eat soup." His smile is crooked. "I would like to spend some time with her. I do not think that a body is required."

"Mr. Cole," says Jian, "the Hall—"

"The Hall does not need me. It has the Nine." He looks round the table. "It needs you. It needs a roll of nine names, and a lamp for each, and a promise that none of you will ever be left alone with it. That is all the Founders ever should have asked."

"And the Gate?"

"I have been keeping it open on my own." He lifts his transparent hand. "It is the last of my burdens. I will hand it to you. All of you. One piece each. It will be heavy, but it will not be unbearable, because you will be nine."

Mo Yan gets to her feet. She walks across the circle and kneels by his chair and takes his silver fingers in both of hers, and puts them against her forehead.

"She says thank you," murmurs Yue, from the wall.

"For what?"

"For waking her up," says Yue. Her voice shakes. "She says it was worth it."

* * *

Ethan Cole dies at dusk, three days later, under the Mother Tree.

It is not a dramatic thing. He walks up the hill on Nurse's arm with the small girl on his other side, and sits on the root where the black soil is warm. He rests his head against the bark. His eyes close. The tree sings, very low, and when it finishes the song, there is no one on the root but an old gray cat that has wandered up from the kitchen, and it curls into the hollow where he sat and goes to sleep.

Nobody speaks for a long time. The sun goes down. The stars come out.

Then Nurse, who has not wept in front of anyone in six hundred years, sits down in the snow and puts her face in her hands.

Little Mei puts one arm around her. She does not say anything. She holds the rabbit up, and Nurse takes it, and holds it, and the three of them sit there in the dusk while the tree sings overhead, and the sleepers breathe in the Hall below, and the stars come out one by one over the valley of the Lins.

* * *

Wenyuan and Qinghe wait for him in the kitchen.

It is the small hours. The fire has burned to red. They sit on either side of the long table, not touching, a broad slow man and a small spotted woman, and between them lies a plate of barley cake that neither has eaten. He knows what it is before he sits. They have been talking about him.

"You look dreadful," says Qinghe.

"Thank you, Mother."

"Eat." She pushes the plate across. "You have not had a proper meal in three days. Your father says you are holding up a whole Hall on your own, and I say you are holding up a whole Hall on cold tea."

"I am not on my own."

"No," says Wenyuan. "That is what we wanted to say."

Jian looks at him. His father's eyes are grave. They are not the eyes of a man who has come to scold. They are the eyes of one who has made up his mind.

"We have decided to go to the Wall," says Wenyuan. "Both of us. At the new moon, with Han's wagons. The clan needs a hand there, and the Hall will not need us once the Nine are settled."

"Father—"

"We are old, Jian." It is said without self-pity. "Older than you know. Your mother and I have lived a good deal longer than the rest of the clan, by the grace of whatever the Founders did to us. We have seen the Hall's lamps go out and come on again. We have seen our son take the weight of a world." He swallows. "It is time we stopped being a weight on you."

"You were never a weight."

"We were a reason," says Qinghe quietly. "And you have not needed a reason for some time. So eat the cake, and go to sleep, and do not argue. Your sister will be here. Your cousins will be here. You will not be alone."

He opens his mouth. Something moves behind his ribs, a small wet knot he cannot name, and the cough rises with it. He lets it come. Qinghe is around the table before he can finish, one broad hand against his back, the other pressing a cloth to his mouth.

"There," she says, when it passes. "There. Hush."

He sits with his head on her shoulder like a child, and she does not move.

"I will come back," he says, muffled. "After the Hall. After..."

"I know."

"I will find a way to stay."

"You always do." She strokes his hair. "That is rather the trouble with you, my son."

Wenyuan clears his throat. Then, awkwardly, he reaches across the table and puts the plate of cake in front of Jian once more, and after a moment Jian takes a bite, and finds that it tastes of home.

* * *

Jian sits on the Dock stair at midnight with a cup of cold tea, and does not drink.

The Hall is quiet. The lamps burn in their rings, fewer than they once were, and a handful of new ones have been lit in the lowest circle where the first sleepers have been brought down to wake. The air smells of bread. Somewhere far below, a woman is laughing, and a man answers her, and a child says something shrill and delighted. It is the sound of a great many people learning how to live again.

He thinks about the Seam. About the Bloom, who has gone home, or whatever the word is for what it has done. It left the cellar open behind it, and the stair of light has gone out, but the voice remains in Mo Yan's palm and Yue's, small and clear and content. It says it will sleep now. It says it will dream of fields.

The Keystone countdown reads, on the edge of his mind, in small plain letters: SUSPENDED.

He lets it.

He is a hundred and five years from death by the Interface's reckoning, and he is coughing blood every day, and he has not slept properly in a month. He is also, for the first time since he woke in this body, not afraid. The thing that was pressing on his skull has become a companion. The weight of the Hall has been divided into nine. The clan has a Roll of the Living that grows by the day.

It is enough, he thinks. For one arc of a life.

"Jian."

He turns his head. Mei is standing at the top of the stair. Her light is stronger than it was, a thin steady silver that has stopped flickering. Behind her, in the dark of the passage, Little Mei is asleep on Hua's shoulder.

"Mei," he says. "It's late."

"I know. I couldn't sleep." She comes down two steps and sits beside him. "I wanted to show you something."

She holds out her hand. In it, bright as a coin, lies the silver leaf from the Mother Tree. It is not whole. Along its edge, a hair-fine crack has opened, and from the crack, very faintly, comes a light that is not silver at all. It is blue.

"It was singing," she says. "A little while ago. Not the lullaby. A different tune. I think it's for you."

Jian takes the leaf.

At once the Interface wakes. There is no flicker this time, no sliding panel. The whole of his vision goes silver, then clear, and he sees the Dock as he has never seen it: ring on ring of gold threads running up into the dark, each one a life, each one connected to a point of light high above the vault. The roof of the Hall has opened. Past it is not rock. Past it is a sky, a vast, glittering, impossible sky, crowded with stairs of pale fire that climb and climb and climb.

```
ARK-7 // DOOR REGISTRY
DOOR 1 ................ HELD
DOOR 2 ................ HELD
DOOR 3 ................ HELD
DOOR 4 ................ HELD
DOOR 5 (THE DOCK) ..... HELD
DOOR 6 (THE HALL) ..... HELD
DOOR 7 (THE SEEDBED) .. OPEN, RESTING
DOOR 8 ................ [UNKNOWN]
DOOR 9 ................ [UNKNOWN]
DOOR 10 ............... [ABOVE]

NOTE: THE NINE WERE NOT NINE.
NOTE: THERE WAS A TENTH.
NOTE: THE TENTH WENT UP.
```

His mouth is dry. He reads the last three lines again.

Then, below the table, in smaller type, a final line appears, as if written by a hand he has never seen and a voice he has never heard:

```
TO WHOEVER REACHES CORE-MID WITH A WORKING HEART:
THE SEAM DOES NOT END AT THE VALLEY.
THE REALMS ABOVE WERE BUILT TO HOLD WHAT WE COULD NOT.
COME UP.
— MA RUO-LIN, DOOR 10
```

Beside him, Mei is watching his face. She does not ask what he has seen.

"It's a long way up," she says quietly.

"It is."

"Will you go?"

Jian closes his fist around the leaf. In the dark, far below, a child laughs, and a bell begins to ring, small and sweet, for the first dawn of a Hall that is learning to wake.

"I think," he says, and finds that for the first time in a year he is not afraid of the answer, "that I have eighty years to decide."
